q: The Lighthouse of Alexandria, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, stood in which Egyptian city?
explain: The Pharos Lighthouse guided ships into the busy port of Alexandria, on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, for many centuries.

q: Which sea borders Egypt to the north?
explain: Egypt's northern coastline lies on the Mediterranean Sea, which also washes the shores of southern Europe and North Africa.

q: The Aswan High Dam, one of the biggest dams in the world, was built across which river?
explain: The Aswan High Dam blocks the Nile in southern Egypt and created the vast Lake Nasser behind it.

q: Which Egyptian queen, the last active pharaoh of ancient Egypt, was allied with Rome's Julius Caesar and Mark Antony?
explain: Cleopatra VII was the last ruler of ancient Egypt before the kingdom became part of the Roman Empire.

q: What is the name of the huge artificial lake created by the Aswan High Dam?
explain: Lake Nasser, named after Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser, stretches from southern Egypt deep into Sudan.

q: The Valley of the Kings, where pharaohs were buried in rock-cut tombs, lies on the west bank of the Nile near which modern Egyptian city?
explain: Luxor, ancient Thebes, sits across the Nile from the Valley of the Kings, where Tutankhamun's tomb was discovered.

q: Which ocean borders Morocco to the west?
explain: Morocco's long western coastline faces the Atlantic Ocean, whose beaches are famous with surfers.

q: Which tree, which grows almost only in southwestern Morocco, produces the prized argan oil used in cooking and cosmetics?
explain: Argan oil is pressed from the nuts of the argan tree, and goats in Morocco are famous for climbing them to eat the fruit.

q: Which Moroccan city is famous for its old town painted bright blue?
explain: Chefchaouen, tucked into Morocco's Rif Mountains, is loved for its blue-painted streets and alleyways.

q: What is the highest mountain in Morocco?
explain: Mount Toubkal, in Morocco's Atlas Mountains, is Morocco's and North Africa's highest peak at 4,167 metres.

q: Which two languages are official in Morocco?
explain: Morocco's 2011 constitution made Arabic and Berber (Amazigh) the official languages; French is also widely spoken.

q: The University of Al Quaraouiyine, founded in 859 and one of the oldest universities in the world, is in which Moroccan city?
explain: Al Quaraouiyine in Fez has taught students for over 1,100 years and is often called the world's oldest university.

q: The windy Atlantic port of Essaouira, with its old sea walls and fortifications, was known for centuries by which other name?
explain: European traders and sailors called Essaouira 'Mogador' for hundreds of years.

q: Which gulf does Nigeria's southern coastline open onto?
explain: Nigeria's coast lies on the Gulf of Guinea, the part of the Atlantic Ocean that borders much of West Africa.

q: Nollywood, the nickname of Nigeria's booming film industry, is a play on which famous American place?
explain: Like Hollywood, Nollywood makes hundreds of films a year, and Nigerian movies are hugely popular across Africa.

q: As the Niger River reaches the sea, it spreads out into a huge swampy region called what?
explain: The Niger Delta is one of the world's great river deltas, a maze of mangrove creeks and fishing villages.

q: Nigeria shares borders with Benin, Niger, Chad, and which country to the east?
explain: Cameroon lies along Nigeria's eastern border, and the two countries share a long frontier.

q: Which Nigerian author wrote 'Things Fall Apart', a classic novel about life in an Igbo village before colonial times?
explain: Chinua Achebe's 'Things Fall Apart', published in 1958, is one of the most widely read African novels ever written.

q: Which giant granite monolith rises beside the road north of Abuja and is a famous landmark of Nigeria?
explain: Zuma Rock, a huge monolith over 700 metres tall, towers beside the road from Abuja towards Niger State.

q: The Benue River is a major tributary of which great West African river?
explain: The Benue is the Niger's largest tributary and meets it at the town of Lokoja in central Nigeria.

q: What is the highest mountain in Kenya?
explain: Mount Kenya, an extinct volcano near the equator, is Kenya's highest peak at 5,199 metres; Kilimanjaro lies just over the border in Tanzania.

q: Which Kenyan lake in the Great Rift Valley is world-famous for its huge flocks of pink flamingos?
explain: Lake Nakuru National Park is one of the best places on Earth to see lesser flamingos standing in pink clouds on the water.

q: The Maasai people of Kenya and Tanzania are famous for wrapping themselves in which colourful cloth?
explain: A shuka is a bright checked cloth that Maasai warriors and elders drape over their shoulders.

q: Which Kenyan city, a historic port on the Indian Ocean, is famous for its Old Town with beautifully carved wooden doors?
explain: Mombasa has been a trading port for centuries, and its Old Town doors are carved with Swahili patterns.

q: The Tana River, the longest river in Kenya, flows southeast into which ocean?
explain: The Tana travels about 1,000 kilometres from the highlands near Mount Kenya to the Indian Ocean.

q: Which Kenyan island town, a UNESCO site where cars are banned and dhows sail in the harbour, is famous for its Swahili culture?
explain: Lamu Old Town, on Lamu Island, has been a Swahili trading centre for more than 600 years.

q: Which country lies along Kenya's northeastern border, with a long coastline on the Indian Ocean?
explain: Somalia stretches along Kenya's northeastern frontier, from the Ethiopian border down to the sea.

q: Cape Agulhas, the southernmost point of the African continent, is where which two oceans meet?
options: The Red Sea and the Mediterranean Sea
explain: By tradition, the Atlantic and Indian Oceans meet at Cape Agulhas, at the very tip of Africa.

q: Afrikaans, one of South Africa's official languages, developed mainly from which European language?
explain: Afrikaans grew from the Dutch spoken by settlers who arrived at the Cape in the 1600s.

q: Which flightless bird, black and white with a loud braying call, breeds on the beaches of South Africa?
explain: African penguins, sometimes called jackass penguins for their donkey-like call, nest at places like Boulders Beach near Cape Town.

q: The Drakensberg, whose name means 'Dragon Mountains', runs along the border between South Africa and which small, mountainous country?
explain: Lesotho, a kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa, is often called the 'Kingdom in the Sky' for its high mountains.

q: Which South African dried meat snack, seasoned with vinegar and spices and similar to jerky, is a national favourite?
explain: Biltong is made by air-drying strips of spiced meat, and beef biltong is sold in shops everywhere in South Africa.

q: Which river forms much of South Africa's northern border before turning east and flowing into the Indian Ocean?
explain: The Limpopo winds north and east across southern Africa, forming borders with Botswana and Zimbabwe.

q: The Big Hole, a huge open-pit diamond mine and famous landmark, is in which South African city?
explain: The Big Hole in Kimberley was dug by hand by thousands of miners during the 1870s diamond rush and is now a museum.

q: The Blue Nile and the White Nile meet at which city?
explain: At Khartoum, the capital of Sudan, the Blue Nile, which rises in Ethiopia, joins the White Nile to form the great Nile.

q: The Blue Nile flows out of which large Ethiopian lake?
explain: Lake Tana, Ethiopia's largest lake, is the source of the Blue Nile, which carries water all the way to Egypt.

q: Which Ethiopian town is famous for its 11 churches carved out of solid rock at Lalibela?
explain: King Lalibela had the churches of Lalibela cut from the pink volcanic rock about 800 years ago, and they are still used today.

q: Which mountain range in northern Ethiopia, a UNESCO World Heritage site, is home to the gelada baboon and the rare Ethiopian wolf?
explain: The Simien Mountains have dramatic cliffs and valleys, and the gelada baboon lives almost nowhere else on Earth.

q: The ancient Kingdom of Aksum, famous for its giant stone stelae, was centered in what is now Ethiopia and which neighbouring country?
explain: Aksum's heartland spanned northern Ethiopia and today's Eritrea, and its tall carved stelae still stand at Aksum.

q: Dallol, in Ethiopia's Danakil Depression, is famous for its colourful landscape of what?
explain: Dallol's boiling springs, yellow sulfur deposits, and salt plains make it one of the strangest and hottest places on Earth.

q: Ethiopia shares borders with Eritrea, Djibouti, Somalia, Kenya, and South Sudan. Which country lies to its west?
explain: Sudan lies along Ethiopia's western border, and the two countries share a long frontier.

q: The Akosombo Dam on the Volta River created which huge lake, one of the world's largest man-made lakes?
explain: Lake Volta is one of the largest reservoirs on Earth by surface area, stretching across much of eastern Ghana.

q: What is the name of the brightly coloured woven cloth traditionally made by the Ashanti people of Ghana?
explain: Kente cloth is woven in narrow strips on a loom and then sewn together, and each pattern can tell a story.

q: The Golden Stool, the sacred symbol of the Ashanti nation, is kept in which Ghanaian city?
explain: Kumasi, the heart of the Ashanti kingdom, is where the Golden Stool is guarded as the soul of the Ashanti people.

q: Ghana is bordered by Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, and which smaller country to the east?
explain: Togo is a narrow country squeezed between Ghana and Benin on the Gulf of Guinea.

q: Mole National Park, in northern Ghana, is best known for which large animals?
explain: Mole National Park is famous for its elephants, which you can watch from a hide as they gather at the waterholes.

q: Lake Bosumtwi, Ghana's only natural lake, fills the crater left by what?
explain: A meteorite smashed into Ghana about a million years ago, and the bowl it left behind filled with rain to form Lake Bosumtwi.

q: Fufu, a beloved staple of Ghanaian meals, is made by pounding which two starchy foods together?
explain: Boiled cassava and plantains are pounded into a smooth dough and eaten with soup, and it takes a strong arm to make it.

q: Which sea borders Algeria to the north?
explain: Algeria's northern coast lies on the Mediterranean Sea, whose shores link Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East.

q: Which Algerian city, perched above a deep gorge and famous for its many bridges, is called the 'City of Bridges'?
explain: Constantine sits on rocky cliffs above the Rhumel River gorge, and its bridges have linked the city for centuries.

q: Which volcanic mountain range in the Sahara, home to the Tuareg people, lies in southern Algeria?
explain: The Hoggar Mountains rise from the Sahara like a rocky island, and Mount Tahat, Algeria's highest peak, is among them.

q: Which Algerian plateau, a UNESCO site, holds thousands of prehistoric rock paintings and engravings in the middle of the Sahara?
explain: Tassili n'Ajjer's sandstone cliffs are covered with paintings of giraffes, elephants, and people from thousands of years ago.

q: Which vast sand sea of huge orange dunes lies in western Algeria?
explain: The Grand Erg Occidental is one of the Sahara's biggest dune fields, a sea of sand that is hard to cross even today.

q: The Chelif River, the longest river that lies entirely within Algeria, flows into which sea?
explain: The Chelif winds about 700 kilometres through northern Algeria before reaching the Mediterranean near Mostaganem.

q: Which Tunisian island, the country's largest, is famous for sandy beaches and the old town of Houmt Souk?
explain: Djerba, in Tunisia's south, has been a trading island for thousands of years and is linked to the mainland by a causeway.

q: Which Tunisian town is home to a huge Roman amphitheatre, one of the best preserved in the world?
explain: The amphitheatre of El Jem, built around 238 AD, could hold about 35,000 spectators for gladiator games.

q: What is the traditional red woollen cap with a black tassel worn in Tunisia called?
explain: The chechia has been part of Tunisian dress for centuries and is still worn at festivals and celebrations.

q: Which group of low-lying islands off Tunisia's east coast is known for fishing, olive trees, and palm groves?
explain: The Kerkennah Islands are flat and quiet, a world away from the busy streets of the mainland.

q: Which Tunisian ruins include a well-preserved Roman theatre, temples, and ancient paved streets?
explain: Dougga, high on a hill in northern Tunisia, is one of the finest Roman towns in North Africa.

q: Which Tunisian salt flat is a vast shallow lake that dries into a white crust in summer?
explain: The Chott el Djerid is so salty that in summer its bed turns into a shimmering white plain.

q: Which Tunisian town, perched on a cliff above the sea, is famous for its white houses with blue shutters?
explain: Sidi Bou Said, just north of Tunis, has been a favourite haunt of artists for over a century.

q: Which Tanzanian island, the largest in the Zanzibar archipelago, is famous for Stone Town and its spice markets?
explain: Zanzibar island, also called Unguja, has been a trading hub for spices like cloves for centuries.

q: Which Tanzanian landmark is a huge volcanic caldera, one of the world's largest, where thousands of animals live on the crater floor?
explain: The Ngorongoro Crater was formed when a giant volcano collapsed, and today lions, elephants, and rhinos roam its floor.

q: Swahili, a language blending Bantu and Arabic words, is the lingua franca of which part of Africa?
explain: Swahili is spoken from Kenya to Mozambique and is the everyday language of millions of East Africans.

q: Which channel separates the island of Zanzibar from mainland Tanzania?
explain: The Zanzibar Channel is a busy stretch of water that ferries shuttle across between the island and the mainland.

q: The Rufiji River, Tanzania's largest river, flows through a huge national park into which ocean?
explain: The Rufiji winds through the great Selous reserve, now Nyerere National Park, where hippos and crocodiles slide into its waters.

q: Tanzania borders Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, DR Congo, Zambia, and Malawi. Which country lies along its southeastern side?
explain: Mozambique stretches along Tanzania's southern border, down to the Ruvuma River.

q: Which Tanzanian gorge, a UNESCO site, is famous for the early human fossils discovered there by the Leakey family?
explain: Olduvai Gorge's layers of rock have yielded some of the oldest human ancestor fossils ever found.

q: Which Senegalese lake is nicknamed the Pink Lake because algae turn its water reddish?
explain: Lake Retba, near Dakar, gets its pink colour from salt-loving algae, and its water is so salty you can float in it easily.

q: What is the name of Senegal's national sport, a traditional form of wrestling?
explain: Laamb, also called Senegalese wrestling, fills stadiums across the country and is hugely popular on television.

q: The Senegal River forms the border between Senegal and which country to the north?
explain: The Senegal River flows west along the border with Mauritania and empties into the Atlantic near Saint-Louis.

q: The Djoudj National Bird Sanctuary, a UNESCO site in the Senegal River delta, is a winter home for migratory birds from which continent?
explain: Every winter, ducks, pelicans, and flamingos fly from Europe to rest and feed in the Djoudj wetlands.

q: Which Senegalese city, built on an island where the Senegal River meets the sea, was once the capital of French West Africa?
explain: Saint-Louis, with its colonial buildings on a narrow island, was the capital of French West Africa until 1902.

q: Which Senegalese national park is a group of rocky islets, a haven for nesting seabirds, off the coast near Dakar?
explain: The Madeleine Islands are a tiny national park where frigatebirds and other seabirds nest on the bare rock.

q: Which Senegalese singer, famous for mbalax music and the duet '7 Seconds', became a global star?
explain: Youssou N'Dour has sold millions of records and performed with artists from all around the world.

q: The Gambia River runs through which narrow country that is almost entirely surrounded by Senegal?
explain: The Gambia is a thin ribbon of a country, never more than about 50 kilometres wide, following the river to the Atlantic.

q: Madagascar is a huge island in which ocean, off the southeast coast of Africa?
explain: Madagascar lies in the Indian Ocean, about 400 kilometres from the coast of Mozambique.

q: Which giant flightless bird, taller than a grown-up, once lived only on Madagascar and is now extinct?
explain: The elephant bird stood up to three metres tall and laid the largest eggs of any bird.

q: Malagasy, the main language of Madagascar, is most closely related to languages spoken on which large island in Indonesia?
explain: Long ago, sailors from Borneo crossed the Indian Ocean and settled Madagascar, and their language became Malagasy.

q: Which Madagascar primate taps on tree bark with a long thin middle finger to find insect larvae?
explain: The aye-aye's extra-long finger lets it drum on wood and pull grubs out of their tunnels, and it is mostly active at night.

q: What is the name of the highest mountain in Madagascar, in the Tsaratanana Massif?
explain: Maromokotro rises to 2,876 metres in the Tsaratanana Massif in the far north of Madagascar.

q: Which Madagascar UNESCO site is a 'forest' of sharp limestone pinnacles called tsingy?
explain: The Tsingy de Bemaraha is a maze of razor-sharp limestone towers where lemurs leap from peak to peak.

q: Madagascar is one of the world's leading growers of which fragrant spice used in cakes and ice cream?
explain: Madagascar grows a large share of the world's natural vanilla, and the orchid flowers are pollinated by hand.
